findings.evidence: template/scripts/requirement_intake.py `claim_started_requirement` calls `requirement_board.reconcile_nonterminal` directly. template/scripts/execute_requirement.py `_claim_card` skips the claim when `observation.current_status == "Done"`. `reconcile_nonterminal` (requirement_board.py:30-48) writes the desired status whenever it differs from the current one, with no Done check. I did not check whether `start_pre_authoring` rejects a closed or Done Requirement earlier. tests/test_requirement_card_claim.py covers the Done case only for `advance`.
findings.summary: The claim in `requirement_intake.py start` has no terminal-status guard, though the `advance` claim does. Rerunning `start` on a Requirement whose card is already `Done` may move it back to `In progress`.

findings.evidence: template/scripts/requirement_intake.py `claim_started_requirement`: `except Exception as exc: raise RequirementIntakeError(...)`. Compare execute_requirement.py `_claim_card`: `except (requirement_board.RequirementBoardError, managed_project_status.ManagedProjectStatusError)`. The test `test_claim_failure_keeps_state_reports_rerun_and_never_writes_ready` injects `RuntimeError`, which only the broad catch handles.
findings.summary: `claim_started_requirement` catches bare `Exception`, while the `advance` claim catches only the board and status error types. The two differ in what they handle, and the broad catch hides programming errors behind a 'rerun' message.
